notes.text: We have not here attempted delineate how each dialect tends to go its own way as to morphosyntactic structures that are used (or not used!) to distinguish among "all x’s, all of x, every, each, the whole", etc.; for which we urge readers to consult the dialect grammars. Instead we have simply chosen to give examples of each type of construction attested for each dialect along with their general semantic force. In general, though, as in other Semitic languages, kl with a singular definite noun means "the entire, the whole x" while "all x’s" may be expressed by using nouns in the singular absolute or plural definite states.

notes.text: DJBA distinguishes "ring" from this word on the basis of the Yemenite vocalization as if equivalent to the Hebrew word kippā and derives it then from the root kpp "to curve" and the meaning from the geonic explanation as Hebrew נזמים. Given the Syriac usage form precious stone "jewelry" and the fact that none of the citations indicate anything about rings rather than simply precious stones, we have not accepted his interpretation. A general semantic confusion with Ɂbn is apparent only in Syriac, otherwise only when used as a material and large, natural stone objects. Generally masculine in the targumim with the clear exception of Targum Proverbs under the influence of the Syriac usage. For a very large list of the types of stones attested in Syriac see PSm-Thes. 1664ff.

Compare, for example, the substantial semantic and stress-position differences between "come nów!" and "cóme now". It is quite possible that in some cases JlAtg מִכְעַן means "therefore" rather then "from now on".

notes.text: Greek κάρον? This word is the etymon of English caraway (from Latin from Arabic), but whether this is the precise aromatic seed originally meant by the Greek is not certain. The plant is native to western Asia, but the word seems variously to have also been used for "fennel" and "cumin" as well, both in antiquity and more recently in various languages. The latter is probably meant in the cited passage from LSt since of the three only cumin seems to have been regularly used externally for medicinal purposes. Flora 3:437f.

citations.translation: the woman who wants to say to her friend "rest by me(?), have some ilk to eat"

notes.text: Neither the actual spelling, the context, nor the the geonic interpretation support DJBA's identification of such a word as a Galilean pronunciation of "milk" with a laryngeal as opposed to a pharyngeal unvoiced fricative. The point of the story is that Galileans did not pronounce their guttural fricatives at all. Indeed, to judge by modern Aramaic, it is in the East where ḥeth was pronounced laryngeally, although there is some evidence for laryngeal pronunciation in the West in non-initial position; See The Akkadian Influences on Aramaic, Assyriological Studies 19 (Chicago: Oriental Institute, 1974)')" onmouseout="toolTip()">AIOA
